language_wrapper: The Bank of Pittsburgh now issues coins placed on an {rows}-by-{cols} rectangular grid. Each coin has a heads side and a tails side. Initially, the grid is a perfect checkerboard of tails-up and heads-up, with the top-left coin tails-up and adjacent coins alternating in orientation. In a move, Vera flips exactly one coin. On the first move, Vera may flip any coin. On all subsequent moves, she may only flip a coin that is orthogonally adjacent (shares an edge) to the coin she flipped on the previous move. Determine the smallest possible number of moves Vera can make to reach a state in which every coin is heads-up.
hardness_rationale: The extension moves from a one-dimensional path of coins to a two-dimensional grid with orthogonal adjacency and a checkerboard initialization. The walk must satisfy vertex-parity demands on a bipartite graph while obeying local adjacency constraints, elevating the problem from a linear traversal to a grid-walk parity design. The minimal move count depends on the parity of the total number of cells, necessitating reasoning about color classes, Hamiltonian traversals, parity balancing, and boundary corrections. This significantly increases complexity over the original AIME seed, where a linear structure and specific parity yielded a single closed form.
notes: Generator favors nontrivial grid sizes and avoids the fully trivial 1x1 (verifier nonetheless handles it). The verifier encodes the parity-based closed form derived from a grid-walk construction and parity lower bounds. Instances with both even and odd area occur frequently, reinforcing the necessity to handle parity edge cases.
source_question:
The Bank of Pittsburgh issues coins that have a heads side and a tails side. Vera
has a row of 7873 such coins alternately tails-up and heads-up, with the leftmost
coin tails-up.
In a move, Vera may flip over one of the coins in the row, subject to the following
rules:
• On the first move, Vera may flip over any of the 7873 coins.
• On all subsequent moves, Vera may only flip over a coin adjacent to the coin
she flipped on the previous move. (We do not consider a coin to be adjacent
to itself.)
Determine the smallest possible number of moves Vera can make to reach a state in
which every coin is heads-up.
